title: The Endless Visitor
premise: Pest controller Tamsin Iversen is called to Hollowmere Farm, where a family has been answering a voice from their well in their sleep — a voice with questions, and lately, answers. Skeptical Tamsin discovers the farm's founders began a sealing ritual generations ago and died before finishing it; the well refills every solstice, and this year it will overflow. To survive, Tamsin must adopt the family she was hired to protect, complete the founders' ritual, and choose between sealing the well forever — which will trap the voice's original speaker, a drowned child, inside — or opening it and letting something older walk free. She finds a third way: she gives the ritual her own name, binding the visitor to her instead of the land, and walks out of Hollowmere carrying it.
about_author: Tamsin Dunmore grew up above a funeral home in coastal Maine, where she learned early that the dead are better company than the living. A former building inspector, she writes horror about houses, work, and the terrible competence of ordinary people.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A routine rodent complaint at Hollowmere Farm turns strange: droppings arranged in spirals, a well cap freshly soldered shut. She quotes a price, pockets a deposit, and leaves. Beat: professional detachment established, first wrongness noted and dismissed.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The farmer, Edda Voss, calls again — the thing in the walls left greasy handprints on the nursery ceiling, small ones, five-fingered. Tamsin finds a print that matches no child in the house. Beat: her skepticism cracks a hairline.

chapters.title: The Voss Family
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with Edda's testimony. Dinner at the farmhouse: Edda, her brother Hal, and his mute daughter Wren, who draws the same face over and over. Tamsin learns the family hasn't slept in separate rooms in a year. Beat: found-family seed planted; she stays the night against her own policy.

chapters.title: Recordings
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Edda plays audio from a baby monitor: Wren asleep, answering questions in a voice not her own. 'What did you bury?' 'Where is the rest of you?' Tamsin hears a second voice reply. Beat: belief arrives as dread, not conversion.

chapters.title: What the Founders Knew
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the county archive she finds the farm's founding ledger — a ritual of nine steps, seven completed, dated 1911. The last founders' entries stop mid-sentence. Beat: the plot's engine revealed; the deadline (solstice, three weeks) established.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Hal's POV. Hal checks the well at dawn: the sealed cap is wet inside, waterline risen six inches overnight. He doesn't tell Edda. Beat: guilt and secrecy fracture the family; reader learns the well 'refills' with something worse than water.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The visitor speaks to Tamsin directly in her motel room — through the smoke detector's chirp pattern. It asks her name. She refuses. Beat: she is now a participant, not a contractor; first personal violation.

chapters.title: Wren's Drawings
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Wren's sketches, dated across a century, show the same drowned child at different ages — the visitor was once a girl the founders failed to save. Tamsin realizes the ritual's final step requires a name freely given. Beat: sympathy for the monster; moral stakes clarified.

chapters.title: Edda's Bargain
chapters.summary: Edda's POV. Edda confesses she's been answering the voice for months, trading small truths for Wren's sleep. The visitor knows things about Hal's past that could end him. Beat: love against duty — Edda has already betrayed the family to protect it.

chapters.title: The Seventh Step
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Following the ledger, Tamsin and Hal locate the founders' cache under the barn: salt, iron, a ledger of names — including, freshly written, Tamsin's own. Beat: the visitor has chosen her; the horror becomes inescapable.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She burns her page from the ledger and drives away, taking a motel two counties over. The visitor follows via every ticking, dripping, humming thing. Beat: flight fails; she understands there is no distance, only completion or surrender.

chapters.title: Hal's Confession
chapters.summary: Hal's POV. Hal admits the family's secret: their grandfather reopened the well in 1974 for the water rights, waking the visitor. The refill is his inheritance. Beat: generational guilt; the family's unity becomes Tamsin's reason to stay.

chapters.title: Wren Speaks
chapters.summary: Wren's POV (rendered as her first spoken words in a year). Wren tells Tamsin the visitor isn't asking to get out — it's asking to be finished, buried properly, mourned. Beat: the mission reframes from exorcism to funeral.

chapters.title: The Eighth Step
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The eighth step requires the founders' bloodline to witness. Edda and Hal agree; the ritual at the well half-succeeds — the water stills, then rises faster. The visitor's grief turns to hunger. Beat: false victory, escalating clock.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV rotation. The farm prepares: salt lines, the ledger, Wren's drawings used as a map of the well's true depth — far deeper than any well. Beat: found family assembles as a unit; calm before the flood.

chapters.title: The Overflow
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The well breaches at midnight; water climbs the walls without spilling, and the drowned child walks out of it, asking her name again, gently, endlessly. Beat: climax begins — the question is no longer a threat but a genuine need.

chapters.title: What Tamsin Buried
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Under pressure, Tamsin admits her own burial: a sister lost young, a name she never says aloud. The visitor recognizes a fellow unfinished grief. Beat: her refusal was always self-protection; the theme of price made personal.

chapters.title: The Ninth Step
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The final step demands a living name given freely to hold the seal — or the seal broken with mourning. Tamsin writes her own name in the ledger, but as mourner, not anchor: she names the drowned child instead, giving the visitor the identity the founders erased. Beat: climax resolves through love, not force.

chapters.title: The Well Goes Quiet
chapters.summary: Edda's POV. The water drains to honest mud. The child's voice says thank you once, in Wren's borrowed timbre, and is gone. Wren speaks her own name aloud for the first time in a year. Beat: release; the family breathes.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She invoices the Vosses for pest control, waives the fee, and stays a week helping repair the barn. The ledger's last page now holds two names, side by side. Beat: found family formalized; the price paid was her isolation.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, months later, in her own apartment. A new recording — her own sleep monitor — captures a second voice answering questions. It is calm, familiar, patient. It asks nothing. Beat: ambiguous coda; the binding holds, but Tamsin is no longer alone, and never entirely will be.

chapters.title: Hollowmere, Revisited
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Spring: she returns to the farm uninvited and is met at the gate by Wren, who was waiting. Inside, Edda has set a fourth plate. The well cap is rusted open and dry, and the wind through it sounds almost like humming. Beat: resolution — she stops being a visitor and becomes family; the endless visitor was, in the end, herself.
